Tap + to add your first piece
Tap + to log your first practice session
Create lists for recitals, concerts, etc.
The pieces will not be deleted.
Add pieces and sessions to see statistics.
Choose a method to add chord sheets:
Import entire folders with song files (.pro, .crd, .txt, .chopro). Ideal for existing song collections.
Copy chords and text from Ultimate Guitar. The app automatically converts it into ChordPro format.
Create a chord sheet manually. Use ChordPro format [C]Text for precise chord placement.
Choose which epochs should appear in selection lists.

Would you like to view the app introduction again?
Klaviatur helps you manage your music repertoire, practice effectively, and organize chord sheets.
Track your pieces with composer, epoch, difficulty, and total bars. Divide pieces into sections and monitor your progress.
Use the practice timer with Focus Mode and built-in metronome. Keep your daily practice streak alive!
Import songs from folders, create playlists, or convert chords directly from Ultimate Guitar. Features auto-scroll while playing!
Create programs for recitals and concerts, and track your practice statistics over weeks and months.

Klaviatur is your personal companion for your music repertoire: manage your pieces, track your learning progress bar by bar, practice with a timer and metronome, and keep all your chord sheets in one place. This tour walks you through the most important features step by step – and you\'ll try the key ones yourself.
You can change the language at any time in Settings.
👆 Tap the highlighted element to continue.

This is the overview of all your pieces. To get you started, two Beethoven example pieces are already set up. Each card shows the title, composer, status (New, Learning, Polishing or Repertoire), key and the difficulty as dots. Pieces are grouped by status: “In progress”, “Repertoire” and “New”.

The colored bar shows at a glance how far along you are with a piece. It is made up of the piece\'s sections, and each color is a learning level: gray = not learned yet, red = learning, turquoise = polishing, green = mastered. The percentage on the right shows how much of the piece is already “Mastered” (green).

Use these chips to filter your repertoire by status, tags and epoch. Tap a chip to filter, and tap it again to remove the filter. You assign your own tags (e.g. #recital) when editing a piece; they then show up here automatically.

The top bar has four helpers: Shuffle picks a random piece to practice, the music-note icon opens the metronome, the gear opens Settings (language, epochs, backups and this tutorial) and the magnifier searches by title or composer. Pieces you haven\'t practiced for a while are also suggested under “Time to refresh!”.

Down here you switch between the areas: Repertoire (where you are now), Practice (timer, focus mode, streak and your practice log), Lists (e.g. programs for recitals), Statistics (practice time, epochs, composers) and Chords (chord sheets). After this tour you can explore everything at your own pace.
You add new pieces with the green plus button. Try it right away: tap the plus.
Type the name of a composer or work here, e.g. “Beethoven”. The app searches the OpenOpus database (internet connection required) and fills in title and composer for you as soon as you tap a result.
Enter the title and composer here (required fields), plus difficulty, epoch and your own tags. The better you maintain these details, the more useful filters and statistics become.
Set the piece\'s status – New, Learning or Repertoire – and optionally a target tempo in BPM. You\'ll see the target tempo later on the piece page; your actual tempo goes into the tempo log.

Attach your sheet music as a PDF or image here – it will then be available right inside the app. If you enter the total number of bars, the progress bar can show your learning status correctly. Don\'t know the bar count? No problem: the automatic bar detection can work it out for you later.
“Save” at the top right creates the piece. We won\'t save anything during this tutorial – just tap “Next” and we\'ll head back to the overview.
Let\'s take a closer look at a piece. Tap the card of Beethoven\'s “Pathétique”.

At the top you see the title, composer, status and difficulty. “Start” starts a practice timer – when you stop it, the session is saved automatically. “Switch to Focus Mode” opens a distraction-free practice screen with a metronome. The pencil at the top right lets you edit all details of the piece.
This is the same progress bar as in the overview – just bigger. Below it you\'ll find your target tempo, if you\'ve set one.

A piece consists of sections, e.g. “Takt 1–10” (bars 1–10). Each section has a learning level (gray, red, turquoise, green) – the progress bar is calculated from them. Tap a section to change its name, bars, level and notes. “+ Section” adds a new one, “Auto-Split” divides the piece into equally long sections automatically. The most convenient way to create sections is directly in the sheet music – I\'ll show you in a moment.
With “+ Entry” you record how fast you last played the piece (in BPM) – optionally with a note. That way you can see your progress in black and white.
In the “Sheet music & PDF” area you attach PDFs or images to your piece. Now tap “View & Edit Sheet Music” to open the score.

At the top you see the piece title, bar count and the current page. On the right: fullscreen hides all bars, the stopwatch starts a practice session and the play icon scrolls the score automatically – ideal when your hands are on the instrument. You then set the speed with the slider at the bottom. Use two fingers to zoom into the score.

Your tools are at the bottom: “Verschieben” (move) for scrolling and selecting bars, “Stift” (pen) and “Marker” (highlighter) for fingerings and highlights (with a color choice), “Radierer” (eraser), “Takt” (bar) for bar detection and corrections, and “Abschnitte” (sections) to show or hide the section display. Everything you draw stays saved.

This bar lists all sections of the Pathétique with their bars and learning level. Once bars have been detected (we\'ll get to that with the second piece), the sections are also marked in color directly on the score – so you can see right away which passages still need work.
Sometimes you want to see the score without any markings. Tap “Abschnitte” (sections) to hide the display.
The bar is gone. Tap again to show the sections once more. The sections themselves are kept – only the display changes. On to the second piece.
Now I\'ll show you the automatic bar detection. For that we\'ll open the second example piece: tap the “Moonlight” sonata.
Open the score here too via “View & Edit Sheet Music”.

To create sections and track your progress bar by bar, the app has to know where each bar starts and ends. The bar detection does this automatically: it looks for the staff systems and barlines in your score scan and numbers every bar. You\'ll find it in the “Takt” (bar) tool.

The bar detection is currently designed for piano systems: two connected staves are recognized as one system. The cleaner and straighter the scan, the better it works. We\'re working on extending the feature to other instruments as well.
Now tap “Takt” (bar) to open the editing mode.
Now for the exciting part: tap “Takterkennung” (bar detection). It only takes a moment.

The app has drawn in the staff systems and barlines: green and red lines frame the systems, blue lines separate the bars. The total number of bars was automatically saved to the piece. Scroll through the score and check that everything looks right.

If something was detected wrongly, you can fix it yourself: “System +” adds a missing staff system (tap its middle), “Taktstrich +” (barline) adds a missing barline, and “Löschen” (delete) removes wrongly detected systems or barlines. You can also tap a line and move it with a long press and drag. Note: running the bar detection again replaces the previously detected lines.

Switch back to “Verschieben” (move). Now you can tap bars (or long-press and drag across several bars) to select them. A bar with “Abschnitt erstellen” (create section) appears at the top: give it a name and a learning level – and the section shows up in color in the score, in the progress bar and on the piece page.
Besides sheet music, Klaviatur also manages chord sheets for guitar, piano and more. Do you want to use this feature? If not, the tutorial ends here – and I wish you lots of fun with the app!

The plus button adds chord sheets. There are three ways: import a whole folder, paste text from Ultimate Guitar, or write a sheet manually in ChordPro format (e.g. [C]text). At the top you search for songs, mark favorites and sort them into playlists. In a song sheet the app can scroll along automatically. Next, let\'s look at the Ultimate Guitar import.
Here\'s how to bring a song over from Ultimate Guitar: open the song there in your browser, select the full text including the chords and copy it. Here you first enter the title and artist.
Paste the copied text into this large field. The app recognizes which lines are chords and converts everything to ChordPro format automatically – the chords then sit at the right spot in the lyrics.
“Save” puts the song into your collection, and you can quickly find it again with the “UG Import” filter. We won\'t save anything now – just tap “Next”.

The folder icon imports whole collections at once: pick a folder with song files in .pro, .crd or .chopro format – the app also searches all subfolders and builds an index (you can rebuild it in Settings). For copyright reasons Klaviatur does not ship any song collections. One well-known example is the OLGA archive (OnLine Guitar Archive); you\'ll find similar collections online. Please respect the terms of use of each archive. Download a collection, unpack it and select the folder here.
You now know the most important features of Klaviatur. Have fun practicing and making music! You can replay this tour at any time in Settings under “Start Tutorial”.
